headline: ChatGPT and Codex usage limits are merging
summary: OpenAI is consolidating usage limits for its popular language models, impacting how developers can access and utilize these powerful AI tools.
details: OpenAI has announced a significant change to its API access, merging the usage limits for ChatGPT and Codex models. This move aims to streamline resource allocation and simplify the user experience for developers working with these AI technologies.

Previously, developers had separate quotas for interacting with ChatGPT for general conversational tasks and Codex for code generation. The consolidation means that usage across both model families will now count towards a single, unified limit.

The exact implications for developers will depend on their specific usage patterns. Those heavily reliant on both models may need to adjust their strategies to stay within the new combined limits. OpenAI has stated this change is intended to optimize performance and availability for all users.

This integration suggests a move towards a more unified AI platform from OpenAI, potentially paving the way for future model developments and access methods. Developers are advised to monitor their API usage closely and consult OpenAI's documentation for detailed information on the new limits.

headline_marked: [[Altoids Tin Project]]: Father and Son Build Tiny Computer
headline: Altoids Tin Project: Father and Son Build Tiny Computer
summary: A father and son duo transformed an Altoids tin into a functional mini-computer, iterating through five versions to achieve their goal.
details: A father and his 12-year-old son embarked on a two-month journey to create a miniature computer housed within an Altoids tin, inspired by a robot kit and a YouTube video.
Their project, dubbed the 'Altoids Project,' began with a free robot kit and a used ThinkPad. They salvaged a 128x64 display but struggled to find its pinout, with AI providing incorrect information.
After finding the correct schematic online, they got the display working and ran the 'Space Trash' game. Inspired by a DIY video, they decided to miniaturize the setup into an Altoids tin.

Switching to an Arduino Nano and using LiPo batteries with a PowerBoost, they faced challenges fitting components. Their son handled all the CAD and 3D printing for custom parts across multiple iterations.
They experimented with solderable breadboards and even a genuine, slightly taller Altoids tin, but struggled to get the lid to close properly in early versions.
A desoldering mishap damaged a display, leading them to order a new one. Further adjustments were needed as the new display didn't default to SPI mode, requiring more soldering.
The breakthrough came with a new soldering iron that provided more even heating, allowing them to finally hot-glue the display and achieve a closing lid in version 4.
Despite initial wire breaks, they refined the connections using ultra-fine wires, with the son taking on most of the soldering and debugging.
The final product, after five iterations and replacing nearly all original components, includes two actual Altoids in the tin for a touch of authenticity.
caption:
A father and son built a working computer inside an Altoids tin, iterating five times to get it just right.

A father and his 12-year-old son embarked on a two-month journey to create a miniature computer housed within an Altoids tin, inspired by a robot kit and a YouTube video.

Their project, dubbed the 'Altoids Project,' began with a free robot kit and a used ThinkPad. They salvaged a 128x64 display but struggled to find its pinout, with AI providing incorrect information.

After finding the correct schematic online, they got the display working and ran the 'Space Trash' game. Inspired by a DIY video, they decided to miniaturize the setup into an Altoids tin.

Switching to an Arduino Nano and using LiPo batteries with a PowerBoost, they faced challenges fitting components. Their son handled all the CAD and 3D printing for custom parts across multiple iterations.

They experimented with solderable breadboards and even a genuine, slightly taller Altoids tin, but struggled to get the lid to close properly in early versions.

A desoldering mishap damaged a display, leading them to order a new one. Further adjustments were needed as the new display didn't default to SPI mode, requiring more soldering.

The breakthrough came with a new soldering iron that provided more even heating, allowing them to finally hot-glue the display and achieve a closing lid in version 4.

Despite initial wire breaks, they refined the connections using ultra-fine wires, with the son taking on most of the soldering and debugging.

The final product, after five iterations and replacing nearly all original components, includes two actual Altoids in the tin for a touch of authenticity.
